lesson.title: Transforming Every Element Without a Loop
lesson.summary: map applies a function to every item of an iterable and hands back an iterator of the results, replacing a common for loop pattern with a single expression.
lesson.body:
A very common task is transforming every element of a sequence the same way: doubling every number, uppercasing every word, converting every string to an integer. Using a for loop, that looks like building an empty list and appending a transformed value on every iteration. Python's built in map function packages that exact pattern into one call: map(function, iterable) applies function to each item of iterable in turn.

Here is the for loop version and the map version side by side, since seeing the equivalence is the fastest way to understand what map is doing:

numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4]

doubled_loop = []
for x in numbers:
    doubled_loop.append(x * 2)

doubled_map = map(lambda x: x * 2, numbers)

Both doubled_loop and doubled_map represent the same values conceptually, but they are not the same kind of object. doubled_loop is a list you can print directly. doubled_map is a map object, an iterator, and this is a change from Python 2, where map returned a list immediately.

Trace what happens when you actually run this:

print(doubled_map)
print(list(doubled_map))

The first print does not show [2, 4, 6, 8]. It shows something like <map object at 0x1035c2a90>, because map is lazy: it has not computed anything yet, it has only set up the instructions for how to compute each value when asked. Calling list() on it forces every item to be produced, so the second print does show [2, 4, 6, 8].

There is a gotcha worth internalizing here: map objects are single use iterators. If you called list(doubled_map) a second time after the first, you would get back an empty list, [], because the iterator has already been exhausted, there is nothing left to produce. This is different from a list, which you can read over and over. If you need to use the transformed data more than once, convert it to a list with list(map(...)) and keep that list around.

You do not always need a lambda as the function argument to map. If a suitable function already exists, you can pass it directly by name:

words = ["cat", "dog"]
print(list(map(str.upper, words)))

Trace: map calls str.upper on each element of words. str.upper("cat") returns "CAT", and str.upper("dog") returns "DOG", so list(...) collects them into ['CAT', 'DOG'], which is what gets printed. Passing str.upper works because it is just a function that expects one string argument, exactly the shape map calls its function with, so no lambda wrapper is needed at all.

map also accepts multiple iterables at once, applying a function that takes that many arguments and stopping as soon as the shortest iterable runs out: list(map(lambda a, b: a + b, [1, 2, 3], [10, 20, 30])) produces [11, 22, 33]. Whether you reach for map or a plain for loop is often a matter of style and readability rather than correctness. map tends to read cleanly when the transformation is a short expression, while a for loop is often clearer once the logic grows beyond one line, which is exactly the tradeoff you already learned about lambdas.
